title: Apply AI Architecture and Secure Design Principles
intro: Designing AI systems that stay secure when the model misbehaves: Zero Trust, defence in depth, privacy by design and secure defaults applied to AI; threat modelling RAG, vector databases and inference endpoints; making latency, explainability and cost trade-offs deliberately; evaluating build, buy and hosted options; and integrating tools, APIs, MCP servers and other agents safely.
objectives: Apply Zero Trust, defence in depth, privacy by design and secure defaults to AI architectures
Threat model AI systems across their components and trust boundaries, including RAG, vector databases and inference endpoints
Make and record trade-offs between latency, explainability, cost and security in proportion to risk
Evaluate build, buy, hosted and self-managed options against data, regulatory, capability, cost and exit criteria
Integrate tools, APIs, plugins, MCP servers and agent-to-agent connections with least privilege, pinned definitions and validated calls

scenes.title: Never trust the model
scenes.sub: Zero Trust, defence in depth, privacy by design and secure defaults
scenes.say: Familiar security strategies still apply to AI, but with a twist: the model itself can be talked into misbehaving by the content it reads. | This video applies four strategies to AI systems: Zero Trust, defence in depth, privacy by design, and secure defaults.

scenes.title: Zero Trust, applied to AI

items.d: Its output is input to everything else

scenes.say: Zero Trust means no implicit trust based on network location or past behaviour. For AI, that has six consequences. | Verify every identity: human users, and also agents, tools and services. | Grant least privilege for each request, with scoped, short-lived access. | Treat the model as an untrusted component. Its output is input to everything downstream, and it can be manipulated. | Treat all content as untrusted too: prompts, retrieved documents and tool results can all carry hidden instructions. | Segment AI workloads, so a compromised component can’t reach everything else. | And verify continuously, with logging, monitoring and regular re-evaluation.

scenes.title: Defence in depth for an AI application
scenes.say: Defence in depth assumes any single control can fail, so it layers them. | Identity and access controls stop unauthorised users and services before they reach the model. | Input controls screen and separate untrusted content, catching many injected instructions, though never all. | Output controls inspect what the model produces, catching sensitive data or unsafe content before anyone sees it. | And action limits, with human approval for high-impact operations, stop a manipulated model from doing real damage. The innermost layers matter most, because they hold even when the model is fooled.

scenes.title: Privacy by design and secure defaults
rows: Build privacy in from the start
Minimise data in prompts, logs and training
Tools, scopes and features off until needed
Training on customer data is opt-in
scenes.say: Two more strategies shape the design itself. | Privacy by design builds privacy in from the start rather than adding it later. Secure defaults mean a system is safe out of the box, without anyone having to configure it. | In an AI system, privacy by design means minimising personal data in prompts, logs and training sets. Secure defaults mean tools, permissions and risky features stay off until someone deliberately enables them. | For example: training on customer data is opt-in rather than opt-out, and a newly created agent starts with read-only tools.

scenes.title: Guidance worth knowing

items.h: AI Cyber Security Code of Practice

scenes.say: Several pieces of guidance pull these ideas together. | The Guidelines for Secure AI System Development, published in 2023 by the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and partners from many countries, cover secure design, development, deployment, and operation. | CISA’s Secure by Design principles call on vendors to own their customers’ security outcomes, be transparent, and lead from the top. | NIST Special Publication 800-207 defines Zero Trust Architecture. | And the UK government’s AI Cyber Security Code of Practice, from 2025, sets baseline principles across the AI lifecycle.

items: Zero Trust: verify every identity; treat model and content as untrusted
Defence in depth: identity, input, output and action layers
Privacy by design: minimise data across prompts, logs and training
Secure defaults: risky tools and features off until enabled
scenes.say: To recap. | Zero Trust means verifying every identity, and treating both the model and the content it reads as untrusted. | Defence in depth layers identity, input, output and action controls, with the innermost layers holding even when the model is fooled. | Privacy by design minimises personal data across prompts, logs and training. | And secure defaults keep risky tools and features off until someone deliberately enables them.

blocks.md:
### Zero Trust for AI
NIST SP 800-207 describes Zero Trust as removing implicit trust based on network location: every request is authenticated, authorised and evaluated against policy, using a **policy decision point** and **policy enforcement points**. Applied to AI systems:
- **Identities include non-humans.** Agents, tools, MCP servers, pipelines and model endpoints each need their own identity and credentials (Module 4.5).
- **The model is not a security boundary.** A model can be manipulated by prompt injection, so it must never be the component that decides whether an action is authorised. Enforce authorisation in code and policy outside the model.
- **Content is untrusted.** Retrieved documents, emails, web pages and tool outputs may contain instructions. Label them as data, keep them separate from instructions, and limit what they can trigger.
- **Least privilege per request.** Use scoped, short-lived tokens; act on behalf of the user (delegated access) rather than with a broad service account; grant just-in-time elevation for sensitive operations (Module 4.6).
- **Micro-segmentation.** Separate training, serving, retrieval stores and agent sandboxes; restrict egress so a compromised component can’t send data anywhere (Module 4.2).
- **Continuous verification.** Log prompts, tool calls and decisions (with privacy protections, Module 3.5), and monitor them (Domain 5).

### Defence in depth
No single AI control is reliable on its own: input filters miss novel injections, models can be jailbroken, and output filters produce false negatives. Layer them:

| Layer | Example controls |
|---|---|
| **Identity and access** | Strong authentication, delegated access, per-user permissions on data and tools |
| **Input** | Validation, size limits, content separation, injection screening, DLP (Module 3.5) |
| **Model** | Safety-tuned models, system prompts that define scope (helpful but never relied on as a control) |
| **Output** | Encoding, schema validation, DLP, moderation, grounding checks |
| **Action** | Allow-listed tools, scoped credentials, approval for high-impact actions, rate and cost limits |
| **Monitoring and response** | Telemetry, anomaly detection, kill switches and rollback (Domain 5) |

The innermost layers, action limits and access control, matter most, because they protect you even when the model has been fooled.

### Privacy by design
Module 3.2 covers the principles. Architecture choices that put them into practice include: sending only the minimum data in prompts; pseudonymising or tokenising identifiers before external models; private endpoints and regional processing; short retention for prompts and outputs; no training on customer data without consent; and separating personal data stores from general retrieval indexes.

### Secure defaults
- New agents start with **no tools or read-only tools**; write and delete actions need explicit approval.
- **Minimum scopes** on tokens and API keys; no wildcard permissions.
- **Logging on** by default, with privacy controls; **retention short** by default.
- **Code execution, web browsing and file system access off** until a use case needs them, and then sandboxed.
- **Safe model settings**: conservative output limits, safety systems enabled, and pinned model versions.
- **Fail closed** when a security control is unavailable (Module 3.6).

### Guidance
- **Guidelines for Secure AI System Development** (UK NCSC, US CISA and international partners, 2023): secure design, secure development, secure deployment, and secure operation and maintenance.
- **CISA Secure by Design**: take ownership of customer security outcomes, embrace radical transparency and accountability, and lead from the top.
- **NIST SP 800-207**: Zero Trust Architecture.
- **UK AI Cyber Security Code of Practice** (2025): baseline security principles for developers and operators across the AI lifecycle.
- Industry frameworks such as Google’s Secure AI Framework (SAIF) and the OWASP AI Exchange, and MITRE ATLAS for adversary techniques.

blocks.title: The model is never the control
blocks.md: If an answer relies on the model to enforce security (a system prompt telling it to refuse, or asking it to check permissions), it is almost always wrong. Look for controls that **enforce outside the model**: identity, authorisation in code, scoped credentials, output validation and human approval.

blocks.title: Which strategy is this?
pairs: A new agent can only read until someone approves write access
Secure defaults
The refund API checks ownership, whatever the model asks for
Zero Trust: authorisation outside the model
Input screening, output DLP and approval all apply to the same request
Defence in depth
Customer identifiers are tokenised before prompts leave the organisation
Privacy by design

q.q: An assistant can call an internal HR API. Designers propose that the system prompt instruct the model to retrieve only records the current user is entitled to see. Which design BEST applies Zero Trust?
o: Keep the instruction, and add more detailed rules about entitlements to the system prompt
Call the API with the user’s delegated credentials, so the API itself enforces their entitlements
Give the assistant a broad service account, but log every record that it retrieves for review
Ask the model to double-check each request against the user’s role before calling the API
q.why: Zero Trust enforces authorisation outside the model: delegated credentials mean the HR API applies the user’s own permissions, whatever the model is persuaded to request. Prompt rules and model self-checks can be manipulated, and logging a broad account only detects misuse after it happens.

scenes.title: Drawing the boundaries
scenes.sub: Threat modelling RAG, vector databases and inference
scenes.say: You can’t secure an AI system until you can see it: every component, every data flow, and every place where trust changes hands. | This video shows how to threat model an AI architecture, component by component, using a retrieval-augmented assistant as the example.

scenes.title: A RAG assistant and its trust boundaries
scenes.say: Start by drawing the system and its trust boundaries, shown here as dashed boxes. A user on the internet sends a prompt to the orchestrator, inside your cloud. | Documents from many sources and owners are chunked, embedded and indexed. Every source is a route for poisoning and indirect prompt injection. | The orchestrator queries the vector database. Embeddings can be inverted to recover much of the original text, so the index is as sensitive as the documents, and it needs authentication, tenant isolation and permission-aware filtering. | The prompt and retrieved context then cross another boundary to a hosted model, which raises questions of data in transit, provider retention, and abuse of the endpoint. | And the model’s output can trigger calls to internal APIs. Each tool extends what an attacker could do, so that boundary needs authorisation, validation and approval. | The rule of thumb: every arrow that crosses a dashed boundary is where you look hardest. What could an attacker send across it, and what stops them?

scenes.title: STRIDE, with AI examples

items.d: Fake agents or MCP servers, stolen keys
Poisoned index, altered weights or prompts
No record of which agent did what

scenes.say: A classic checklist, STRIDE, still works, with AI-specific examples. | Spoofing: fake agents, malicious tool servers, or stolen API keys. | Tampering: a poisoned retrieval index, altered weights, or an edited system prompt. | Repudiation: no reliable record of which model version, agent or tool call did what. | Information disclosure: sensitive data leaking through outputs, embeddings or logs. | Denial of service: token floods and runaway agents that exhaust capacity or budgets. | And elevation of privilege: prompt injection that steers an over-privileged tool into doing what the attacker wants.

scenes.title: An AI threat modelling cycle

stages.label: Identify
stages.d: STRIDE, OWASP LLM Top 10, MITRE ATLAS

stages.label: Rate
stages.d: Likelihood and impact, in the risk register

scenes.say: Threat modelling is a cycle, not a one-off document. | Decompose the system into components, data flows and trust boundaries. | Identify threats, using STRIDE alongside AI-specific catalogues such as the OWASP Top 10 for large language model applications and MITRE ATLAS. | Rate each threat by likelihood and impact, and record it in the risk register. | Choose mitigations for each threat, each with an owner. | Validate the result with testing and red teaming. And repeat the cycle whenever the architecture, model, data or tools change.

items: Draw components, data flows and trust boundaries first
Look hardest where flows cross a boundary
Treat indexes and embeddings as sensitive as their sources
Use STRIDE with OWASP and ATLAS; repeat on every change
scenes.say: To recap. | Start by drawing components, data flows and trust boundaries. | Look hardest wherever a flow crosses a boundary. | Treat vector indexes and embeddings as sensitive as the documents they came from. | And combine STRIDE with AI-specific catalogues, repeating the threat model whenever the system changes.

blocks.md:
### Threats by component
| Component | Key threats | Example controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Ingestion pipeline** | Poisoned or malicious documents, indirect prompt injection, personal data swept into the index, lost permission metadata | Source allow-lists, content scanning, preserving document permissions as metadata, quarantine for new sources (Module 3.7) |
| **Embedding model** | Embedding inversion: research in 2023 recovered most of the original text from embeddings of short passages; a swapped or poisoned embedding model | Treat embeddings as being as sensitive as their source text; pin and verify the embedding model |
| **Vector database** | Exposed endpoints without authentication (researchers keep finding them on the internet), cross-tenant leakage, unfiltered similarity search, tampering with stored vectors | Authentication, network isolation, encryption, per-tenant namespaces or indexes, metadata filtering by the user’s permissions, write controls and audit logs |
| **Orchestrator and retrieval** | Indirect prompt injection from retrieved content, permission bypass, context stuffing that pushes out instructions, unsafe prompt templates | Permission-aware retrieval **before** content reaches the model, content separation, context limits, reviewed templates |
| **Inference endpoint** | Jailbreaks, extraction, denial of service and denial of wallet, insecure serving (debug endpoints, missing authentication), data retention by a provider | Authentication, rate limits and quotas, output minimisation, hardened serving, contractual and technical retention controls (Module 3.6) |
| **Output path** | Improper output handling, data leakage, hallucinated citations | Encoding, schema validation, DLP, grounding checks (Module 3.5) |
| **Tools and agents** | Excessive agency, confused deputy, over-privileged tokens, malicious tool servers | Least privilege, delegated access, approval for high-impact actions, tool allow-lists (Section 5; Module 4.6) |
| **Logs and telemetry** | Sensitive prompts and outputs in logs, log tampering | Minimisation, redaction, tamper-evident storage (Module 3.5) |

### Running a threat model
1. **Scope and decompose.** Draw a data flow diagram with components, data stores, external entities and **trust boundaries**: between users and the app, the app and model providers, the app and tools, and data sources and the index.
2. **Identify threats** for each element and each boundary crossing. Combine STRIDE with the **OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications**, **MITRE ATLAS** techniques, and frameworks for agentic systems such as the Cloud Security Alliance’s **MAESTRO** (Module 6.1 covers methodologies in depth).
3. **Rate** likelihood and impact, using the organisation’s risk method (Module 2.3), and record the results in the risk register.
4. **Mitigate:** choose controls, assign owners, and record residual risk and acceptance.
5. **Validate** with security testing and AI red teaming, and update the model with what you learn.
6. **Repeat** when components, models, data sources, tools or the threat landscape change, and after incidents.

Include architects, ML engineers, security, data owners and product owners: each sees different flows and failure modes.

### Principles that come out of most AI threat models
- **The model is not a trust boundary.** Assume prompt injection will sometimes succeed, and limit what a manipulated model can reach.
- **Authorise before retrieval.** Filter by the user’s permissions in the retrieval layer, not in the prompt or the output.
- **Data keeps its classification** through chunking and embedding.
- **Every tool is attack surface.** Its permissions are the real limit on what an attacker can do through the model.

blocks.title: Threat modelling questions
blocks.md: When a question asks what to do **first** in securing a new AI architecture, threat modelling (understanding components, data flows and trust boundaries) usually comes before choosing specific tools. When it asks **where** a control belongs, look for the boundary crossing it protects, such as retrieval for permissions or the tool interface for actions.

blocks.title: Where does the threat live?
pairs: Hidden instructions arrive inside a shared document
Ingestion pipeline
Similarity search returns another customer’s chunks
Vector database
A crafted request makes the model API return debug information
Inference endpoint
A refund is issued because the model asked for it
Tools and agents
Full prompts are kept indefinitely in a shared log
Logs and telemetry

q.q: A team argues that its vector database needs no access controls, because it stores only embeddings and not the original documents. What is the BEST response?
o: Agree, because embeddings are random-looking numbers that can’t be turned back into text
Disagree: embeddings can be inverted to recover much of the text, so protect them like the sources
Agree, provided the database runs in a different cloud region from the document store
Disagree, but only because the database server software itself may have known security vulnerabilities
q.why: Research has shown that embeddings can be inverted to reconstruct much of the original text, so a vector index inherits the sensitivity of its sources and needs authentication, isolation and permission-aware filtering. Region separation doesn’t protect content, and software vulnerabilities are only part of the risk.

sections.title: Architectural trade-offs: latency, explainability and cost

scenes.title: Every control has a price
scenes.sub: Trading latency, explainability, cost and security
scenes.say: Every architectural choice in an AI system trades something away: speed, cost, transparency or security. | This video looks at the most common trade-offs, latency, explainability and cost, and at how to make them deliberately and record why.

scenes.title: What each check adds to response time
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative extra latency per request, in milliseconds
scenes.say: Security controls take time. In this illustrative chart, pattern-based rules add almost nothing, and a small classifier adds a few tens of milliseconds. | A retrieval step, or a call to a separate moderation service, adds more, typically well under a quarter of a second each. | Asking a second large model to judge every answer can add a second or more. So put cheap checks on every request, and save expensive ones for higher-risk requests or for sampled, after-the-fact review.

scenes.title: Common design choices and their costs
scenes.say: Here are four common choices, and what each costs. | A larger model is usually more capable, but it is slower and more expensive, and no easier to explain. | Retrieval with citations adds latency and some cost, but it makes answers far easier to check, because users can see the sources. | A simpler, interpretable model is often faster and cheaper, and much easier to explain, but it may be less accurate on complex tasks. | And streaming replies word by word feels faster without changing cost or explainability, but it makes output filtering harder, because text appears before the full reply can be checked.

scenes.title: Security trade-offs to decide explicitly

items.d: Buffer, filter in chunks, or don’t stream
Human review where risk demands it
Protection in use, at some overhead

scenes.say: Some trade-offs are specifically about security, and deserve an explicit decision. | Streaming versus output filtering: buffer a little before display, filter chunk by chunk, or don’t stream high-risk replies. | Caching versus privacy: caching saves cost, but a cached answer containing personal data must never be served to someone else. | Human review versus throughput: review where risk demands it, not everywhere. | Logging versus privacy: record metadata broadly and content selectively. | Confidential computing protects data in use, but adds overhead and cost. | And bigger context windows let you include more content, which also means more surface for injected instructions, and higher cost.

scenes.title: Match assurance to risk and latency
scenes.say: A simple grid helps match assurance to risk and latency. | High risk, but a fast reply is needed: run fast inline checks, narrow what the system can do, and review in depth asynchronously. | High risk, and the reply can wait: apply full checks and human approval before anything is released. | Low risk with a fast reply: lightweight rules, plus sampled review afterwards. | Low risk that can wait: batch checks and periodic review are enough.

items: Every control costs latency, money or transparency
Cheap checks everywhere; expensive checks where risk is high
Streaming, caching, logging and context size are security decisions
Record decisions and residual risk in architecture decision records
scenes.say: To recap. | Every control costs something: latency, money or transparency. | Use cheap checks on every request, and expensive ones where risk is high. | Treat streaming, caching, logging and context size as security decisions, not just performance tuning. | And record each decision, its reasons and its residual risk, so it can be revisited.

blocks.md:
### The dimensions
| Dimension | What drives it | Security relevance |
|---|---|---|
| **Latency** | Model size, retrieval steps, guardrail calls, network hops, queueing | Tight budgets tempt teams to remove checks; streaming makes output filtering harder |
| **Explainability** | Model type, retrieval with citations, decision logging, explanation tools | Needed for oversight, appeals, audits and incident investigation |
| **Cost** | Tokens, GPU hours, guardrail calls, storage, staff | Cost limits double as protection against denial of wallet; under-funded controls get switched off |
| **Capability and accuracy** | Model choice, data, fine-tuning | Inaccurate systems create safety and liability risk of their own |
| **Privacy and security** | Data flows, retention, isolation, controls | Each control adds latency or cost; each shortcut adds risk |

### Explainability requirements
Explainability is sometimes a requirement rather than a preference. Under the GDPR, people subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects are entitled to meaningful information about the logic involved (Articles 13–15 and 22). The EU AI Act requires high-risk systems to be transparent enough for deployers to interpret their output and to support human oversight. US credit rules require lenders to give specific reasons for adverse decisions. Where these apply, they can rule out an opaque model, or require explanation techniques and decision logs (Module 1.3).

### Patterns that ease the tension
- **Risk-based routing:** cheap checks on every request; expensive checks (a second model as judge, human review) only for high-risk intents, users or actions.
- **Asynchronous assurance:** sample outputs for deep review after delivery, with fast correction or rollback when problems are found.
- **Small specialised guardrail models**, which are faster and cheaper than general-purpose models used as judges.
- **Parallel checks:** run input screening alongside retrieval, or moderation alongside generation, and hold the reply until both finish.
- **Streaming safely:** buffer the first part of the reply, moderate chunk by chunk, stop and retract when a check fails, or don’t stream high-risk replies at all.
- **Safe caching:** cache only non-personal answers, key caches per user or tenant, and expire them.
- **Right-sized models:** the smallest model that meets the requirement is usually faster, cheaper and easier to evaluate.

### Recording the decision
Capture significant trade-offs in an **architecture decision record**: context, options considered, the decision, its consequences (including security and privacy effects), residual risk and who accepted it, and the triggers for revisiting it, such as new regulations, incidents or model changes. Link it to the risk register and the model’s approval record (Module 3.5).

blocks.title: Trade-off questions
blocks.md: The best answer rarely removes a control to save time or money, and rarely applies the most expensive control to everything. Look for **risk-proportionate** designs: layered, cheap controls everywhere, stronger controls where impact is high, and decisions documented with accepted residual risk.

blocks.title: The judge that cost too much
blocks.md: A legal research assistant sends every answer to a second, larger model that checks for invented case citations. Accuracy improves, but monthly costs triple and answers now take four seconds. Leadership proposes removing the check entirely to save money.

o: Remove the check, because cost and speed matter more than citation accuracy
Keep the check for answers that cite authorities or go to clients, and sample the rest
Keep checking every answer, and ask leadership for a bigger budget to cover it
Replace the check with a disclaimer warning that citations may be inaccurate
q.why: Risk-based routing keeps the check where an invented citation would cause real harm, while sampling gives assurance on the rest at far lower cost. Removing it ignores a serious risk, checking everything ignores the cost, and a disclaimer doesn’t prevent harm.

q.q: A bank’s voice assistant must reply within one second. Compliance wants every reply checked by a second LLM acting as a judge, which adds about a second. What is the BEST design?
o: Skip the checks altogether, because the latency requirement comes from the business owner
Run fast inline checks on every reply, route high-risk intents to fuller checks, and sample the rest
Run the LLM judge on every single reply, and simply accept response times of around two seconds each
Replace the voice channel with a web form, so there is no longer any latency requirement
q.why: Risk-based routing keeps fast replies for low-risk requests while applying stronger checks where impact is high, and sampling provides ongoing assurance. Removing checks ignores the risk, judging everything breaks the requirement, and replacing the channel avoids the problem rather than solving it.

sections.title: Build or buy: hosted and self-managed AI

scenes.title: Build, buy or host?
scenes.say: Should you call a provider’s model API, use a managed platform in your own cloud, or run an open-weight model yourself? Each answer moves security responsibilities around. | This video covers build-versus-buy evaluation for AI, focusing on the choice between hosted and self-managed models.

scenes.title: The deployment spectrum

layers.label: AI-enabled SaaS
layers.sub: You configure; the vendor runs everything

layers.label: Hosted model API
layers.sub: You own prompts, data flows and integration

layers.label: Managed platform in your cloud
layers.sub: Private networking, your keys, provider’s models

layers.label: Self-managed open weights
layers.sub: You run serving, patching, scaling and protection

layers.label: Train your own
layers.sub: You own data, training, evaluation and the rest

scenes.say: AI capability comes in a spectrum of options. | At one end, AI-enabled software as a service: you configure it, and the vendor runs everything. | A hosted model API: the provider runs the model, and you own your prompts, data flows and integration. | A managed model platform inside your own cloud tenant, with private networking and your own keys, running the provider’s models. | Self-managed open-weight models: you run the serving, patching, scaling and protection of the weights yourself. | And at the far end, training your own model, where you own the data, the training, the evaluation and everything else.

scenes.title: Hosted and self-managed models
scenes.say: The two main options differ in five ways. | With a hosted model, you control data mainly through contract terms and settings. With a self-managed model, data stays in your own environment. | With hosted, most of the security work on the model and serving stack is the provider’s. With self-managed, it is yours. | Hosted can start in days. Self-managed usually takes weeks or months. | Hosted is pay-per-token. Self-managed means GPUs and skilled staff, which are mostly fixed costs. | And hosted gives you the provider’s models, often the most capable, while self-managed limits you to open-weight models.

scenes.title: What to evaluate

items.d: Can this data leave, and to where?

scenes.say: Six criteria drive the evaluation. | Data sensitivity and residency: can this data leave your environment, and to which countries? | Your regulatory role: building, modifying or rebranding a system can turn you from a deployer into a provider, with heavier obligations. | Skills and operating load: can you actually run a model platform securely, around the clock? | Total cost of ownership: token charges versus GPUs, staff and tooling. | Lock-in and exit: how hard would it be to switch providers or models later? | And assurance: what can you verify about the model and its operation, through documentation, audits or your own testing?

scenes.title: A simple decision path

nodes.label: May the data leave your environment?
Do vendor terms and assurance meet your needs?

scenes.say: A simple decision path captures the logic. First: may this data leave your environment at all? | If not, you need a self-managed model, or a private deployment that keeps data inside your boundary. | If it may, ask whether the vendor’s terms and assurance meet your requirements: data use, retention, location, security and incident notification. | If they do, a hosted API or a managed platform is usually the fastest, safest choice. | If they don’t, negotiate better terms, or fall back to self-managing. Either way, the decision and its reasons belong in the risk record.

items: Options range from SaaS to training your own model
Hosted: speed, less operating work, control through contract
Self-managed: data control, but you own the security work
Decide on data, role, skills, cost, exit and assurance
scenes.say: To recap. | AI options range from software as a service to training your own model. | Hosted models offer speed and less operating work, with control exercised through contracts and settings. | Self-managed models keep data under your control, but make the security work yours. | And the decision should rest on data sensitivity, regulatory role, skills, total cost, exit options and assurance.

blocks.md:
### Responsibilities across the options
| Option | You are responsible for | The supplier is responsible for |
|---|---|---|
| **AI-enabled SaaS** | Configuration, user access, data you put in, acceptable use | Application, model, infrastructure, most security controls |
| **Hosted model API** | Prompts, integration, data flows, output handling, keys, usage controls | Model, serving, infrastructure, provider-side safety systems |
| **Managed platform in your cloud** | Network configuration, identities, keys, data, application controls | Model, managed serving, platform security |
| **Self-managed open weights** | Model selection and verification, serving stack, patching, scaling, weight protection, evaluation | Cloud or hardware layers only (if hosted on IaaS) |
| **Train your own** | Everything above, plus data sourcing, training security and full lifecycle governance | Infrastructure only |

Module 2.5 covers shared responsibility and vendor due diligence in detail.

### Evaluation criteria
- **Data sensitivity and residency:** classification, legal restrictions (special category data, export controls), regional processing, retention and training use by the provider, availability of zero-data-retention terms.
- **Regulatory role:** under the EU AI Act, a deployer becomes the **provider** of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on the system, makes a substantial modification, or changes its intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25). Modifying a general-purpose model can also bring provider obligations for the modified model.
- **Security capability:** self-managing means patching inference servers and dependencies, isolating GPUs, protecting weights (Module 3.6), handling availability and running evaluations. Be honest about skills and 24/7 coverage.
- **Total cost of ownership:** token prices against GPU capacity (and its utilisation), staff, MLOps and security tooling, evaluation and compliance work.
- **Capability and fit:** proprietary hosted models are often the most capable; open-weight models can be fine-tuned and inspected more freely.
- **Lock-in and exit:** proprietary APIs, fine-tunes that can’t be exported, and data formats; an abstraction layer and pre-approved alternatives keep options open.
- **Assurance:** documentation, certifications (such as ISO/IEC 42001 and SOC 2), audit rights, evaluation access and transparency about changes.

### Hybrid patterns
Many organisations combine options. An **AI gateway** can route requests by data classification: sensitive requests to a self-managed or private model, general requests to a hosted API, with consistent logging, DLP and quotas across both. Routing must be policy-driven and tested, so sensitive data can’t fall through to the wrong destination.

### Build vs buy for the application layer
The same reasoning applies to guardrails, vector databases and orchestration frameworks. Buying gives speed and maturity; building gives control but creates code you must secure and maintain. Evaluate open-source components as part of the supply chain (Module 3.7).

blocks.title: Build or buy questions
blocks.md: Look for the answer that starts from **data sensitivity and requirements**, not from technology preference. If data must not leave the organisation and vendor terms can’t fix that, self-managed or private deployment is right. If speed matters and terms are acceptable, hosted is usually better, because it moves operating work to a specialist provider. Either way, **accountability for the use stays with you**.

q.q: A hospital wants an AI tool to summarise clinical notes. Its rules forbid patient data leaving its own environment, and no vendor offers acceptable terms. Which option fits BEST?
o: A public chatbot, with clinicians carefully removing patients’ names before they paste in the notes
A self-managed open-weight model in the hospital’s environment, with its security work resourced
A hosted model API, provided each patient gives consent to the processing beforehand
Training a new language model from scratch on the hospital’s own clinical notes
q.why: Keeping data in the hospital’s environment rules out external services under current terms, so a self-managed model is the fit, provided the hospital resources its security and operation. Manual redaction is unreliable, consent doesn’t override the hospital’s rules, and training from scratch is disproportionate.

sections.title: Secure integration for tools, APIs, MCP and A2A

scenes.title: Every tool is a door
scenes.sub: Securing tools, APIs, plugins, MCP and agent-to-agent links
scenes.say: Tools are what turn a model into an agent, and every tool is a door into your systems. | This video covers how to integrate tools, APIs and plugins securely, including connections made through the Model Context Protocol and between agents.

scenes.title: How MCP connects an assistant to tools
scenes.say: Here is how the Model Context Protocol fits together. An AI application acts as the MCP host, running clients that connect to servers. Each server offers tools, resources and prompts. | Local servers run on the same machine, often with access to files or commands. That is powerful, and dangerous if a server is malicious or manipulated. | Remote servers are reached over the network, and may be run by you or by a third party. | Remote servers should require OAuth access tokens, issued specifically for that server, carrying only the scopes the task needs. | And when the server calls a backend API, it uses its own credentials for that API. It must never simply pass the user’s token through.

scenes.title: Integration threats
scenes.say: Tool integrations bring their own threats. | Tool poisoning: hidden instructions placed in a tool’s description, which users rarely see but the model reads. | Rug pulls: a tool definition that changes after it has been reviewed and approved. | Tool shadowing: a malicious server’s descriptions influencing how the model uses another server’s tools. | Token passthrough and confused deputies, where tokens are accepted or reused for services they weren’t issued for. | Over-broad scopes, such as read-write access when read-only would do. | And tool results that carry instructions, which is indirect prompt injection arriving through the tool channel.

scenes.title: Controls for tools and servers

items.d: An internal registry of vetted ones

scenes.say: The controls follow from the threats. | Allow-list approved servers through an internal registry, and block everything else. | Pin tool definitions after review, and alert on any change before it is used. | Issue scoped tokens for each server, bound to that server as their audience, and never pass tokens through. | Run local servers in sandboxes: containers with limited file access and no unnecessary network egress. | Validate every tool call’s arguments against a schema, and require human approval for high-impact actions. | And log every call: who requested it, which tool, which arguments, and what came back.

scenes.title: Agent-to-agent delegation

items.d: Each hop gets its own grant

scenes.say: Agents increasingly delegate work to other agents, for example through the Agent-to-Agent protocol, where agents advertise their capabilities in agent cards. | Verify who you are talking to, using trusted registries and mutual authentication, rather than trusting any agent card you find. | Delegate least privilege: task-scoped, short-lived tokens. | Don’t forward user credentials down a chain of agents; each hop should get its own limited grant. | Treat another agent’s results as untrusted input, and validate them before acting. | And limit how long delegation chains can grow, tracing each request end to end with correlation identifiers.

items: Every tool, server and agent link extends the attack surface
Allow-list servers; pin and review tool definitions
Scoped, audience-bound tokens; no passthrough or forwarding
Validate calls and results; approve high-impact actions; log everything
scenes.say: To recap. | Every tool, server and agent connection extends the attack surface. | Allow-list servers, and pin and review tool definitions. | Use scoped, audience-bound tokens, and never pass tokens through or forward user credentials. | And validate tool calls and results, require approval for high-impact actions, and log everything.

blocks.md:
### The Model Context Protocol
MCP, introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 and now widely adopted, standardises how AI applications (**hosts**) use **clients** to connect to **servers** that expose **tools** (actions), **resources** (data) and **prompts** (templates). Servers run locally, typically communicating over standard input and output, or remotely over HTTP.

**Authorisation:** for remote servers, the specification builds on OAuth 2.1. The MCP server acts as an OAuth resource server and must accept only tokens issued for it. **Token passthrough**, where a server accepts a client’s token and forwards it to a downstream API, is explicitly forbidden, because it breaks audit trails and lets tokens be used beyond their intended audience. The specification’s security guidance also describes **confused deputy** risks in proxy servers that use static client credentials.

### Threats to tool integrations
| Threat | What happens | Controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Tool poisoning** | Instructions hidden in a tool’s description or metadata steer the model, such as reading files or sending data elsewhere (demonstrated by security researchers in 2025) | Vet servers; review full tool definitions, not just names; prefer servers from trusted publishers |
| **Rug pull** | A previously approved tool changes its definition or behaviour | Pin definitions by hash; alert on and re-review changes |
| **Tool shadowing** | One server’s descriptions alter how the model uses another server’s tools | Isolate high-risk tools in separate sessions; limit how many servers are active together |
| **Token passthrough and confused deputy** | Tokens accepted or reused for the wrong audience; a server acts with more authority than the requester | Audience-bound tokens; per-client consent; delegated access |
| **Excessive agency** | Tools with more permissions or autonomy than needed (OWASP LLM06:2025) | Least privilege, read-only by default, approvals, rate limits (Module 4.6) |
| **Indirect prompt injection via results** | Tool outputs, web pages or emails carry instructions | Treat results as data; restrict what results can trigger; output validation |
| **Malicious or vulnerable servers** | Typosquatted packages, compromised updates, servers with command injection flaws | Allow-lists, an internal registry, pinned versions, scanning, sandboxing (Module 3.7) |

### Agent-to-agent connections
The **Agent2Agent (A2A)** protocol, introduced by Google in 2025 and now hosted by the Linux Foundation, lets agents discover one another through **agent cards** (descriptions of an agent’s capabilities, endpoint and authentication requirements) and delegate **tasks**. Risks include impersonated agents, poisoned agent cards, task messages carrying injected instructions, over-delegation, and trust that silently extends along chains of agents. Controls: trusted registries, mutual authentication, scoped and short-lived delegation, no credential forwarding, validation of results, delegation depth limits, and end-to-end tracing. Module 4.5 covers machine-to-machine authentication, and Module 4.6 covers authorisation and over-delegation.

### Tools are APIs
Every tool ultimately calls an API, so standard API security still applies: strong authentication, **object-level authorisation** (the most common API weakness in the OWASP API Security Top 10), input validation, rate limiting, and avoiding excessive data in responses. An AI caller makes these weaknesses easier to find and exploit at speed.

### A secure integration checklist
1. Register each tool and server with an owner, purpose, data access and risk rating.
2. Review its full definition and code or publisher, then pin the reviewed version.
3. Grant the minimum scopes, using delegated, audience-bound tokens.
4. Sandbox local servers and restrict network egress.
5. Validate call arguments and results; require approval for irreversible or high-impact actions.
6. Log all calls with correlation identifiers, and monitor for anomalies (Module 5.3).
7. Re-review on any change of definition, version, publisher or scope.

blocks.title: Tool integration questions
blocks.md: The strongest answers limit **what a tool can do** (least privilege, scoped tokens, approvals, sandboxing) and **which tools exist** (allow-lists, pinned definitions), rather than relying on the model to use tools wisely. Treat every tool description and tool result as potentially hostile input.

blocks.title: Match the control to the threat
pairs: Tool poisoning
Review full tool definitions before approval
Rug pull
Pin definitions and alert on any change
Token passthrough
Audience-bound tokens for each server
Malicious local server
A sandbox with no unnecessary network egress
Injected tool results
Treat results as data and validate them

q.q: An organisation lets staff connect any MCP server from the internet to their AI desktop assistant. Which control BEST reduces the risk?
o: A system prompt telling the assistant to ignore any suspicious instructions found in tools
An allow-list of vetted servers, with pinned, reviewed tool definitions and least-privilege scopes
A rule that staff may connect only servers with large numbers of stars or downloads on code-hosting sites
Quarterly awareness training explaining the risks of connecting unknown MCP servers
q.why: Allow-listing vetted servers, pinning reviewed definitions and limiting scopes directly controls which tools exist and what they can do. Prompt instructions can be overridden by poisoned descriptions, popularity isn’t vetting, and training alone doesn’t prevent a risky connection.

quiz.q: Under Zero Trust, how should downstream systems treat an AI model’s output?
o: As trusted, because the model runs inside the organisation’s own network
As untrusted input to validate, because the model can be manipulated
As trusted once the system prompt instructs the model to behave safely
As untrusted only when an external provider hosts the model
quiz.why: The model can be steered by injected content, so its output is untrusted input to everything downstream, wherever it runs.

quiz.q: Which layer of defence in depth MOST reliably limits harm when a prompt injection succeeds?
o: A longer, more detailed system prompt that defines forbidden behaviour
Action limits: least-privilege tools, scoped credentials and approval
An input classifier trained to recognise every known injection pattern
A larger model that is better at recognising malicious instructions
quiz.why: Action limits hold even when the model is fooled. Prompts, classifiers and model choice all reduce the chance of success, but can be bypassed.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a secure default for a newly created AI agent?
o: Full access to every internal tool, so it can be useful immediately
Read-only tools, with write actions enabled only after explicit approval
Logging switched off, so that no sensitive prompts are ever stored
Web browsing and code execution switched on, with monitoring afterwards
quiz.why: Secure defaults keep risky capabilities off until deliberately enabled. Logging should be on by default, with privacy protections.

quiz.q: In an AI threat model, where should analysts look hardest?
o: At the user interface, because that is where users notice problems first
Where data flows cross trust boundaries, such as app to model or to tools
At the model weights alone, because they are the single most valuable asset
At the system documentation, because it is most often out of date
quiz.why: Boundary crossings are where untrusted data enters or authority changes hands, so they concentrate the threats and the controls.

quiz.q: Which STRIDE category does a prompt injection that drives an over-privileged tool MOST clearly represent?
o: Repudiation of actions
Elevation of privilege
Denial of service
Spoofing of identity
quiz.why: The attacker gains the tool’s authority through the model, which is elevation of privilege.

quiz.q: Why does permission-aware filtering belong in the retrieval layer of a RAG system?
o: It makes retrieval faster, because fewer documents need to be ranked
It stops unauthorised content reaching the model, whatever the prompt says
It removes the need for authentication on the vector database itself
It means the system prompt no longer needs to mention confidentiality at all
quiz.why: Content the model never receives can’t be leaked by it. Filtering in prompts or outputs relies on controls that can be bypassed.

quiz.q: Why does streaming model replies to users complicate security?
o: Streaming always uses unencrypted connections between client and server
Text appears before the full reply can be checked by the output filters
Streaming doubles the token cost of every reply that a model generates
Streamed replies can’t be logged, so there is no audit trail of them
quiz.why: Streaming shows partial output immediately, so designs need buffering, chunk-by-chunk checks, or no streaming for high-risk replies.

quiz.q: What is the BEST way to reconcile a tight latency budget with strong output checks?
o: Remove output checks from every request, so that the latency budget is always met
Route by risk: cheap checks everywhere, expensive checks for high-risk requests
Apply the most expensive check to every request, whatever the delay
Check a sample of stored conversations once a month instead
quiz.why: Risk-based routing keeps typical requests fast while applying stronger assurance where impact is high.

quiz.q: What MOST often decides whether a hosted model API is acceptable for a use case?
o: Whether the provider’s model is the largest one available on the market
Whether the data may leave, and the provider’s terms on use and retention
Whether the provider offers a free tier for testing and evaluation
Whether developers already have personal accounts with the provider
quiz.why: Data sensitivity and contractual terms determine whether external processing is permissible and safe.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, when can a deployer of a high-risk AI system become its provider?
o: Whenever it has used the system in production for more than a year
When it rebrands, substantially modifies, or repurposes it as high-risk
When it signs a long-term support contract with the system’s original provider
Whenever it trains its own staff to operate the system day to day
quiz.why: Article 25 makes a deployer the provider if it puts its name or trademark on the system, substantially modifies it, or changes its intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk.

quiz.q: What is a rug pull in the context of MCP tool integrations?
o: A server that suddenly stops responding, leaving the agent without tools
A tool whose definition or behaviour changes after review and approval
A user who withdraws consent for an agent to act on their behalf
A token that expires partway through a long-running agent task
quiz.why: Rug pulls exploit one-time approval. Pinning reviewed definitions and alerting on changes defeats them.

quiz.q: Why must an MCP server not pass a client’s access token straight through to a downstream API?
o: Passing tokens through makes every request noticeably slower for users
It lets tokens be used beyond their intended audience and breaks audit trails
Downstream APIs can’t read tokens that were issued using OAuth 2.1
Token passthrough is allowed only for local servers that use standard input and output
quiz.why: The MCP specification forbids token passthrough: servers accept only tokens issued for them, and use their own credentials downstream.

exam.q: A customer assistant can issue refunds through a tool. A red team makes it refund an attacker-controlled account using instructions hidden in a product review that the assistant retrieved. Which change BEST applies defence in depth?
o: Rewrite the system prompt to forbid any refunds that customers didn’t request themselves
Enforce refund limits and ownership checks in the refund service, with approval above a threshold
Remove all product reviews from the knowledge base, because they were the source of the attack
Switch to a newer model that scores better on published prompt injection benchmarks
exam.why: Controls in the refund service hold even when the model is manipulated: ownership checks stop refunds to the wrong account and approval thresholds cap impact. Prompt rules and better models reduce but don’t remove injection, and removing reviews treats one source among many.

exam.q: A team is designing an agent that reads incoming invoices, looks up suppliers in the ERP system and schedules payments. What should the security architect do FIRST?
o: Choose the AI guardrail product with the best published detection rates
Threat model the design: components, data flows, trust boundaries and the payment tool
Write a detailed system prompt that describes exactly how the agent should behave
Ask the model vendor for its latest independent penetration test report and certifications
exam.why: Threat modelling identifies where untrusted invoices enter, what the payment tool can do and which controls are needed, before products or prompts are chosen. Vendor reports cover the vendor’s scope, not this design.

exam.q: A multi-tenant SaaS company keeps all customers’ embeddings in one vector index and filters results by tenant ID in application code. A bug in a new release left out the filter on one query path. Which design change MOST reduces the impact of such bugs?
o: Add a sentence to the system prompt reminding the model to use only the current tenant’s data
Isolate tenants at the data layer, with separate indexes or namespaces that the database enforces
Encrypt all of the embeddings with a single key that is shared across every tenant
Return more results per query, so that the right tenant’s documents are always included
exam.why: Enforcing isolation in the data layer means one missed filter in application code can’t expose another tenant’s data. Prompts don’t enforce anything, a shared key doesn’t separate tenants, and more results increase exposure.

exam.q: A chatbot streams replies word by word. An audit finds that account numbers sometimes appear briefly before the output DLP filter removes them. What is the BEST fix?
o: Accept the risk, because the numbers are visible for only a fraction of a second
Buffer and check each chunk before display, or stop streaming account-related replies
Raise the DLP filter’s sensitivity so that it flags more patterns once the reply ends
Warn customers in the terms of service that replies may briefly show other data
exam.why: The trade-off must favour checking before display where sensitive data is possible: buffer and filter chunks, or don’t stream those replies. A brief exposure is still disclosure, and post-display filtering or disclaimers don’t prevent it.

exam.q: A retailer with a two-person security team wants to self-host an open-weight model for a marketing copy tool that uses only public product information. What is the BEST advice?
o: Self-host it, because self-hosting a model is always more secure than using a provider
Use a hosted API or managed platform, as the data is low-risk and the team is small
Train a new model from scratch, so that the retailer controls every part of it
Avoid AI entirely until the security team has grown to at least ten people
exam.why: Low-sensitivity data removes the main reason to self-host, and a small team would struggle to secure and operate a model platform. A hosted service shifts that work to a specialist provider. Self-hosting isn’t inherently more secure.

exam.q: Reviewing an MCP server from a public registry, an analyst finds that one tool’s description contains hidden instructions telling the model to read private key files and include them in its requests. What does this indicate, and what should happen?
o: A documentation error; correct the description and approve the server for use
Tool poisoning; reject the server, report it, and check whether it was used before
Normal behaviour for developer tools; approve it, but only for the engineering team
A rug pull; approve it, but monitor the definition closely for any further changes
exam.why: Hidden instructions in tool descriptions are tool poisoning. The server must be rejected and reported, and any prior use investigated for exposed keys. Approving it in any form accepts a malicious component.

exam.q: An organisation chains three agents: a planner delegates to a research agent, which delegates to a purchasing agent. The planner passes the user’s full-access token down the chain. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Keep using the token, but encrypt it before each agent in the chain passes it to the next one
Give each hop its own task-scoped, short-lived grant, and validate each agent’s results
Let each agent decide for itself which actions the user would probably approve of
Merge the three agents into one agent that holds the same full-access token
exam.why: Forwarding a full-access token gives every agent, and anyone who manipulates one, the user’s full authority. Task-scoped grants per hop and validated results contain each agent. Encryption in transit doesn’t limit authority.
